assessmentSummary.identity: A High Front Support Shape Hold starts on a stable floor or mat with both palms and forefeet fixed, straight elbows, shoulders over wrists, ribs and pelvis organized, glutes active, and heels reaching back. It counts only valid continuous hold seconds and ends by controlled knee lowering. It is not a forearm plank, a scapular push-up or protraction hold, a push-up, a bear hover, a limb-lift plank, a moving plank-to-pike cycle, raised or unstable support, an assessment, or a clinical intervention.
currentCardFindings: Source 75 identifies a straight-arm hand-support hold, whereas existing Front Plank variants use bilateral forearm support; these are not interchangeable identities.

The source omits exact contacts, hold validity, entry and exit, anatomy, dosage, fatigue, relationships, quality gates, stop rules, media review, and calibration; this candidate supplies those contracts without inferring participant skill or readiness.

Three direct YouTube search results are stored only as unverified, non-embedded media candidates. Search visibility does not verify playback, exact task match, accessibility, quality, safety, reviewer, or approval.

proposedLoadProfile.recovery: candidate planning estimate only; recompute from actual valid seconds, tension, symptoms, and overlapping hand-support, pressing, crawling, and trunk work

proposedDosage.rest: 30-90 seconds or enough to restore exact support, breathing, and shape
proposedDosage.durationRule: include floor setup, demonstration, valid and failed hold seconds, rest, substitutions, cleaning, and controlled exit

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when exact palm-and-forefoot support, straight elbows, stable floor access, wrist/shoulder/trunk tolerance, communication, current fatigue and impact budgets, duration, logistics, and downstream demands fit. Changing support, elbow action, limb contact, height, instability, load, motion, intent, symptoms, or substitution reruns selection, logistics, duration, fatigue, relationships, persistence, and validation.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Source 75 lineage, high-plank shoulder/scapular activity research as adjacent load context, task mechanics, and comparison with forearm plank, scapular push-up, push-up, bear-hover, and moving high-plank families.
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: No source establishes universal hand or foot spacing, body line, tension, hold duration, recovery, readiness, safety threshold, outcome, transfer, or Vortex score. Independent human calibration remains required.

alternateAssessments.name: High Front Support Shape Hold
alternateAssessments.rationale: This is the exact fixed palm-and-forefoot, straight-arm hold contract.

alternateAssessments.name: Shorter Quality Hold or Longer Rest
alternateAssessments.rationale: Duration and rest change delivery while contacts and shape remain exact.

alternateAssessments.name: Forearm Plank
alternateAssessments.rationale: Forearm support changes wrist loading, elbow position, shoulder angle, base, and task contract.

alternateAssessments.name: High-Plank Scapular Protraction Hold
alternateAssessments.rationale: Required scapular protraction changes action, tension intent, quality gate, and stimulus.

alternateAssessments.name: Knee-Supported High Plank
alternateAssessments.rationale: Knee rather than forefoot support changes load distribution, lower-body contacts, and fatigue.

alternateAssessments.name: High-Plank Limb Lift or Shoulder Tap
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing contact or adding a limb action changes laterality, anti-rotation demand, count, and failure modes.

alternateAssessments.name: Push-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Elbow flexion and extension add vertical displacement, pressing phases, and a repetition count.

alternateAssessments.name: Raised, Unstable, or Loaded High Plank
alternateAssessments.rationale: Support height, instability, or external load changes equipment, mechanics, logistics, fatigue, and risk.
